title: Differentiable Simulators and Policy Gradients
one_liner: Switching between different gradient methods based on whether the model is smooth prevents bias and noise problems when learning robot control policies.
lead: When teaching a robot to do a task, you can estimate the right adjustments to make using calculus on a differentiable model (smooth math), or you can guess at the adjustments by trying random changes (no calculus needed). This paper asks: when the robot's real physics has sudden breaks or jumps, which method actually works better—calculus fails because it assumes smooth slopes that do not exist at discontinuities, while guessing works but is slow—and what's the simplest way to switch between them?

problem.h2: Smooth math breaks on jumpy physics
paras: A reinforcement learning agent (a robot or game player) learns by adjusting numbers called weights. Two methods exist: calculus-based (compute the exact direction to move a weight using the math of the model) and guess-based (try random changes and see what sticks). Calculus is usually faster because it points directly toward better weights.

But real physics is not smooth. A ball rolling might suddenly hit a wall and stop instantly—no gradual transition. When the physics has these sudden jumps, the calculus method fails: the gradient (the direction to nudge a weight) becomes wrong or undefined, biasing the learning. Older work tried to catch these breaks by looking at the noise around the guess-based estimates, but that method is slow, noisy itself, and requires hand-tuned numbers per task.

callout.html: Detect when the physics jumps, then swap from calculus to guess-based gradients in those moments; add a careful variance controller to keep updates stable.

panels.title: 2. Physics hits a jump, calculus breaks

steps.text: Compute calculus-based gradient and guess-based gradient on every step.
Look at where the two estimates disagree strongly—sign of a discontinuity.
In smooth regions, use calculus; at jumps, use guess-based.
Scale the weight nudge by the variance of recent updates.
Move weights, measure reward, loop until policy converges.

paras: The paper changes which gradient estimator (calculus-based vs. guess-based) the algorithm uses on each step, and how much it scales the update.

hidden.name: discontinuity indicator
paras: This is a number that measures how jumpy the physics is at each moment. Instead of looking directly for jumps (which is hard to detect), the paper infers discontinuity from the disagreement between the two gradient methods: if calculus and guess-based give opposite signs or very different magnitudes, the physics is likely jumping.

The paper estimates this by comparing the calculus-based gradient to the guess-based gradient; where they diverge, a switch to the guess-based method is safer. Later, the per-step variance controller (how much the recent updates have changed) becomes the second hidden signal: high variance means instability, so shrink the step; low variance means stable learning, so step bigger.

heat.caption: Darker shows higher disagreement between gradient methods, indicating a jump.

reads.html: The discontinuity indicator is just the disagreement: calculus gradient versus guess-based gradient. If they point in opposite directions, the physics is jumping.

Detect bias in the differentiable simulator by comparing 1st-order (calculus) and 0th-order (guess-based) estimators; switch to 0th-order in nonsmooth regions via DDCG test, or apply per-step inverse-variance weighting (IVW-H) to stabilize variance without explicit discontinuity detection.

paras: Calculus-based gradients are fast because they use the math of the smooth model. But when physics jumps, that math is wrong: a derivative (a slope) does not exist at a jump. The guess-based method is slower and noisier, but it just tries random changes and sees what works—it does not rely on smooth math, so jumps do not break it.

By detecting where the two methods disagree (a sign of a jump) and swapping to guess-based, the algorithm avoids the bias trap. Then, the per-step variance controller (inverse-variance weighting) adjusts how big each weight nudge is based on how much recent updates have wiggled. When updates are shaky (high variance), take smaller steps; when updates are smooth (low variance), take bigger steps. This prevents the noise of guess-based gradients from derailing learning.

stages.s: Current policy weights and recent experience
Compare them; detect jumps if they disagree
Pick the safe estimator: calculus if smooth, guess-based if jump
Scale the update by inverse variance

math.words: Weight update equals the chosen gradient multiplied by a step size scaled by the inverse of recent update variance.
symbols: either calculus or guess-based gradient, picked via discontinuity test
variance of the last N weight updates

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Scenario: smooth region, calculus gradient is reliable.
Update = 0.1 * 100 * 0.8 = 8.0 -> this is a big, confident step in a stable region.
Update = 0.1 * 5 * 0.8 = 0.4 -> step shrinks to 0.4 when updates are shaky.

math.note: The inverse variance weighting automatically brakes the algorithm when updates get noisy (a sign of discontinuities), without needing to detect jumps explicitly.

charts.title: Naive approach (calculus only)
charts.note: Calculus-based gradients excel on smooth tasks but fail when physics jumps.

charts.title: This paper (DDCG + IVW-H)
charts.note: Switching and variance control work on both smooth and discontinuous tasks without per-task tuning.

items.html: If the test for disagreement is too slow or threshold-sensitive, the algorithm might use the wrong gradient for a few steps, accumulating error before the switch.
The discontinuity threshold and inverse-variance scaling constant must both be chosen; if they fight each other, learning becomes unstable.

items.b: Noisy guess-based gradients in small batches.
items.html: Guess-based gradients estimate direction by testing random perturbations and averaging the results across many samples. In low-data regimes (small batches), the average contains too much noise relative to the true direction, so the swapped estimates become unreliable even though they are unbiased.
The paper shows that a single hyperparameter (the discontinuity threshold in DDCG) is sufficient, and IVW-H adapts variance scaling automatically, reducing sensitivity to task-specific tuning.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple robot control task with one region of smooth physics and one region with a sudden discontinuity (e.g., rolling until it hits a wall and stops). Run three learners: calculus only, guess-based only, and the paper's DDCG plus IVW-H. Plot the policy reward over time for each. The demo should show calculus failing in the jumpy region, guess-based working but slowly, and the hybrid method learning fast on both.
demo.metric_eq: final_reward = sum of accumulated rewards from task start to completion, divided by number of steps
demo.closing: The hybrid method should reach 70% final reward in both regions within the same training budget; pure calculus should drop below 50% in the jumpy region.
